entry.title: Oncohistones, part 1: the K27M mutation
entry.content:
This is the first in a set of posts working through the biology of oncohistones. The topic connects to the question I studied in my PhD, how cells hold or lose a chromatin state, so I’m writing up each piece as I read into it. K27M is where the field began, so it comes first.

What an oncohistone is

An oncohistone is a mutation in a histone gene that contributes to cancer. It is a striking idea for two reasons. First, mutant H3 makes up only a minority of the histone H3 pool, yet H3K27M can alter chromatin across the genome. Second, the mutation is in the histone itself, the surface that modifications are written on, rather than in the enzyme that writes them. Many cancer drivers affect enzymes or tumour suppressors; here, the substrate itself is altered.

Oncohistone mutations came to prominence in 2012 through reports in pediatric brain tumors. In their cohort, Wu and colleagues found a lysine-27-to-methionine change (K27M) in 78% of diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas (DIPGs) and 22% of non-brainstem pediatric glioblastomas.2 In a separate cohort, Schwartzentruber and colleagues reported H3.3 K27M as well as mutations at position 34 (G34R/V).1

What K27M does

Lysine 27 on histone H3 can carry H3K27me3, a repressive mark associated with silencing developmental genes. PRC2 writes this mark through its catalytic subunit, EZH2. K27M-containing histone binds EZH2 and inhibits PRC2 methyltransferase activity.3

The effect is not simply that PRC2 can no longer bind chromatin. K27M disrupts the broad spreading of PRC2-mediated H3K27 methylation. H3K27me3 is greatly reduced genome-wide, but can persist at specific loci, including CpG-island-associated sites.5 Reduced H3K27me3 and DNA hypomethylation contribute to altered gene-expression programs in these tumors.4

Why the tumour still needs PRC2

K27M broadly suppresses PRC2 activity, but residual EZH2 activity can still support tumor growth in preclinical models; inhibiting EZH2 slowed growth in those studies.6 This suggested a potential therapeutic vulnerability, but it is not the mechanism of dordaviprone. In 2025, the FDA granted accelerated approval to dordaviprone for adults and children aged 1 year and older with H3 K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma that has progressed after prior therapy. This was the first FDA approval of a systemic therapy for this tumor type. In the FDA efficacy population of 50 patients, the objective response rate was 22%.7

The cell it happens in

A genome-wide loss of repression could in principle affect many cell programs, so cellular context matters. Single-cell RNA-seq of K27M gliomas identified several malignant cell states, including an oligodendrocyte precursor cell-like (OPC-like) state that was highly proliferative.8 The tumor is therefore better described as a collection of cell states than as one precursor population; the OPC-like compartment is particularly proliferative and may contribute to tumor growth.

Open questions

The shape of it: one residue, an inhibited enzyme, a mark that is depleted but persists at some loci, and several tumor cell states. The next posts look at the G34 mutation, which sits next to K27 but works differently, and at whether these tumors buffer the disruption or simply tolerate it.

References

  1. Schwartzentruber J, et al. Driver mutations in histone H3.3 and chromatin remodelling genes in paediatric glioblastoma. Nature. 2012;482(7384):226-231.
  2. Wu G, et al. Somatic histone H3 alterations in pediatric diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas and non-brainstem glioblastomas. Nat Genet. 2012;44(3):251-253.
  3. Lewis PW, et al. Inhibition of PRC2 activity by a gain-of-function H3 mutation found in pediatric glioblastoma. Science. 2013;340(6134):857-861.
  4. Bender S, et al. Reduced H3K27me3 and DNA hypomethylation are major drivers of gene expression in K27M mutant pediatric high-grade gliomas. Cancer Cell. 2013;24(5):660-672.
  5. Harutyunyan AS, et al. H3K27M induces defective chromatin spread of PRC2-mediated repressive H3K27me2/me3 and is essential for glioma tumorigenesis. Nat Commun. 2019;10(1):1262.
  6. Mohammad F, et al. EZH2 is a potential therapeutic target for H3K27M-mutant pediatric gliomas. Nat Med. 2017;23(4):483-492.
  7. U.S. Food and Drug Administration. FDA grants accelerated approval to dordaviprone for diffuse midline glioma. 2025. FDA announcement.
  8. Filbin MG, et al. Developmental and oncogenic programs in H3K27M gliomas dissected by single-cell RNA-seq. Science. 2018;360(6386):331-335.
entry.summary: A single lysine-to-methionine swap in histone H3 can reshape chromatin and gene expression across a cancer cell.

entry.title: What Spatial-Mux-seq Adds to Tissue Epigenomics

link.title: What Spatial-Mux-seq Adds to Tissue Epigenomics

entry.content:
One challenge in tissue epigenomics is connecting regulatory measurements to the location and state of the cells that produced them. Spatial-Mux-seq, published in Nature Methods in 2025, addresses this by measuring five modalities in a spatially resolved tissue section: two histone modifications, chromatin accessibility, whole-transcriptome RNA, and a panel of proteins.

I found the approach interesting because it puts several molecular measurements into a shared tissue context. That makes it possible to study relationships among modalities without relying only on comparisons between separately sampled sections.

What the authors report

The authors applied Spatial-Mux-seq to mouse embryos and mouse brains. Their analyses describe spatial and developmental relationships among histone modifications, chromatin accessibility, gene expression, and protein abundance during neuron differentiation. They also report a radial-glia niche with spatially dynamic epigenetic signals.

These are relationships observed across modalities and tissue locations. They are not, by themselves, proof that one molecular event causes another or a minute-by-minute timeline of differentiation. That distinction matters when interpreting methods that measure several features in the same specimen: co-occurrence and spatial pattern can sharpen a hypothesis, while causal order generally requires additional evidence.

The study’s central technical contribution is the simultaneous, spatially resolved measurement of two histone modifications, chromatin accessibility, whole-transcriptome RNA, and proteins. The method was demonstrated in mouse tissues; applying it to other tissues or experimental questions would require considering its protocol, resolution, and sensitivity for each modality.

What I took from it

Spatial-Mux-seq illustrates why keeping tissue context can matter in epigenomic studies. A molecular profile detached from its location may miss differences between neighboring populations. At the same time, measuring more modalities does not automatically make interpretation simpler: each assay has its own signal properties, and associations across layers still need careful analysis.

For me, the useful lesson is to match a method to the question. If the question concerns how multiple molecular layers are distributed in tissue, a multiplexed spatial assay may offer information that separate assays cannot. If the priority is maximum sensitivity for one modality, a dedicated assay may be more appropriate.

Spatial-Mux-seq measures chromatin modifications, accessibility, gene expression, and proteins simultaneously in spatial context. The study describes relationships among these layers during mouse neuron differentiation and in a radial-glia niche.

   
Paper: Guo et al., Nature Methods (2025) Read the paper →

Reference

  • Guo P, et al. Multiplexed spatial mapping of chromatin features, transcriptome and proteins in tissues. Nat Methods. 2025;22(3):520-529. doi:10.1038/s41592-024-02576-0
entry.summary: One challenge in tissue epigenomics is connecting regulatory measurements to the location and state of the cells that produced them. Spatial-Mux-seq, published in Nature Methods in 2025, addresses this by measuring five modalities in a spatially resolved tissue section: two histone modifications, chromatin accessibility, whole-transcriptome RNA, and a panel of proteins.

entry.title: What Sequencing Methods Teach Us About Inference

link.title: What Sequencing Methods Teach Us About Inference

entry.content:
When I started learning computational biology, I thought of computation as something that happened after an experiment: sequence the sample, then analyze the data. Reading the history of sequencing methods changed that view. In methods such as bisulfite sequencing, the biological quantity of interest is not read directly. It has to be inferred from a measurement shaped by the chemistry and the assay.

That is a useful way to read methods papers: follow the steps from the molecular event to the signal, then from the signal to the biological claim.

Bisulfite sequencing: a chemical conversion, then an inference

Frommer and colleagues introduced genomic sequencing with sodium bisulfite to map 5-methylcytosine at individual DNA strands.1 Under bisulfite treatment, unmethylated cytosines are deaminated and read as thymines after amplification and sequencing, while 5-methylcytosines are relatively resistant and are generally read as cytosines.

The sequence is therefore an assay-dependent readout, not a direct label of methylation. At a cytosine position, a C in the treated read is interpreted as methylated and a T as converted, subject to conversion efficiency, sequencing error, coverage, and alignment. The result depends on both the chemical treatment and the computational steps used to map reads and summarize calls.

Standard bisulfite sequencing also does not distinguish 5-methylcytosine (5mC) from 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC): both are generally read as C. Methods such as oxidative bisulfite sequencing or TAB-seq were developed to distinguish these modifications.2,3

One detail I had not appreciated at first is that a measured conversion is not automatically a perfect classification. Incomplete conversion can make an unmethylated cytosine appear protected; damage or sequencing error can also affect calls. The assay’s chemistry and quality controls are part of the interpretation, not merely preparation before “the real analysis.”

ATAC-seq: more than peak locations

ATAC-seq uses Tn5 transposase to insert sequencing adapters into accessible chromatin.4 The locations of insertions can be used to identify regions enriched for accessibility. The reads also retain fragment-length information, which can reflect nucleosome-associated patterns in the underlying chromatin.

That information needs careful interpretation. Fragment length is not a direct image of a nucleosome, and transcription-factor footprinting is sensitive to factors such as Tn5 sequence bias, coverage, and analysis choices. Methods such as NucleoATAC use fragment patterns to infer nucleosome positioning and occupancy; those inferences depend on the model and data quality.5

The broader lesson I take from ATAC-seq is to ask what information an assay records beyond its most familiar summary. A peak set is one representation of the data, not necessarily the only one. Additional analyses can be informative, but should be validated and described as inferences.

ChIP-seq: modeling the data-generation process

ChIP-seq peak calling offers another example. Enriched read coverage is evidence for protein-associated DNA fragments, but coverage varies for reasons beyond binding. Peak callers therefore compare observed signal with a background model rather than treating every region with many reads as a binding site.

MACS was developed to identify enriched regions in ChIP-seq data using a model of fragment size and local background, with control data used when available.6 The particular model and settings matter; a peak is a statistical call under those assumptions, not proof by itself that a protein directly binds a regulatory element or controls a nearby gene.

The habit I am trying to build

These methods have helped me think of computational analysis as part of experimental reasoning. For any assay, I try to ask:

  • What molecular property does the assay measure directly?
  • What transformations occur between the sample and the data?
  • Which parts of the result are measured, and which are inferred?
  • What technical effects could produce a similar signal?
  • What independent evidence would strengthen the interpretation?

This is not a checklist that guarantees a correct conclusion. It is a way to make the reasoning visible—from chemistry and read generation through analysis to interpretation. That has been a more useful introduction to computational thinking for me than the idea that it begins when a biologist opens a programming language.

References

  1. Frommer M, et al. A genomic sequencing protocol that yields a positive display of 5-methylcytosine residues in individual DNA strands. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 1992;89(5):1827-1831. doi:10.1073/pnas.89.5.1827
  2. Booth MJ, et al. Quantitative sequencing of 5-methylcytosine and 5-hydroxymethylcytosine at single-base resolution. Science. 2012;336(6083):934-937. doi:10.1126/science.1220671
  3. Yu M, et al. Base-resolution analysis of 5-hydroxymethylcytosine in the mammalian genome. Cell. 2012;149(6):1368-1380. doi:10.1016/j.cell.2012.04.027
  4. Buenrostro JD, et al. Transposition of native chromatin for fast and sensitive epigenomic profiling of open chromatin, DNA-binding proteins and nucleosome position. Nat Methods. 2013;10(12):1213-1218. doi:10.1038/nmeth.2688
  5. Schep AN, et al. Structured nucleosome fingerprints enable high-resolution mapping of chromatin architecture within regulatory regions. Genome Res. 2015;25(11):1757-1770. doi:10.1101/gr.192294.115
  6. Zhang Y, et al. Model-based analysis of ChIP-Seq (MACS). Genome Biol. 2008;9(9):R137. doi:10.1186/gb-2008-9-9-r137

Reading the history of sequencing methods changed that view. In methods such as bisulfite sequencing, the biological quantity of interest is not read directly. It has to be inferred from a measurement shaped by the chemistry and the assay.

entry.title: Learning to Think Beyond a Linear TET Pathway

link.title: Learning to Think Beyond a Linear TET Pathway

entry.content:
I first learned DNA methylation through a tidy set of arrows: 5-methylcytosine (5mC) is added to DNA, TET enzymes oxidize it, and further processing can contribute to demethylation. That outline is useful, but it left me thinking about methylation as a switch and the TET enzymes as interchangeable parts.

Reading the early TET literature made that picture harder to hold. The original biochemical work showed that TET1 can convert 5mC to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC).1 Later studies showed that TET proteins can further oxidize 5mC to 5-formylcytosine (5fC) and 5-carboxylcytosine (5caC); 5caC can be excised by thymine DNA glycosylase (TDG), providing a route toward DNA demethylation.2,3 These findings describe biochemical possibilities; they do not mean every modified cytosine passes through every state in the same way, in every cell.

What does 5hmC tell us?

I used to think of 5hmC mainly as an intermediate on the way to demethylation. That remains one possible interpretation, but it is not the only one. Studies in mouse embryonic stem cells reported that TET1 and TET2 contribute to 5hmC production and linked 5hmC with pluripotency and lineage specification.4

The presence of 5hmC alone does not tell us whether it is transient, relatively stable, or associated with a particular regulatory outcome. Those interpretations depend on context and on what is measured. The point that changed my thinking was narrower: a mark detected in a sample should not automatically be assigned a single function from the pathway diagram alone.

This also made me more careful with the familiar shorthand that methylated DNA is “off” and unmethylated DNA is “on.” DNA methylation can be associated with transcriptional repression, but expression depends on genomic location and other regulatory factors. A methylation measurement, by itself, is not a complete readout of gene activity.

Similar enzymes, distinct contexts

The three TET enzymes share catalytic activities, but that does not make them interchangeable in every biological setting. Their expression patterns and functions can vary by cell type and developmental context.4,5 A phenotype following loss of one enzyme also cannot, by itself, tell us whether another enzyme compensated.

For example, a TET1 knockout study reported that loss of Tet1 was compatible with embryonic and postnatal development in mice, while also documenting phenotypes.5 I had initially read results like this as evidence of redundancy. The more careful interpretation is that the organism can develop without TET1 under the conditions studied; identifying why requires additional evidence. Compensation is one possibility, not a conclusion supplied by viability alone.

A different way to read a pathway

The change for me was not abandoning pathway diagrams, but treating them as starting points. When I read a paper or think through an experiment, I try to separate the biochemical step from the cellular outcome:

  • What reaction is directly established?
  • Where and in which cell type was it measured?
  • Is the proposed effect on gene expression measured, or inferred?
  • What other mechanisms could explain the observation?

These questions are part of what I mean by computational thinking. They do not require a computer; they require making assumptions visible and asking whether the available evidence distinguishes between explanations.

I am still learning how to apply this way of thinking across epigenetic measurements and how to communicate uncertainty without obscuring the result. For me, the most useful habit has been to say precisely what a study shows, what it suggests, and what remains open. A pathway diagram can orient the question. It cannot replace the evidence needed to answer it.

References

  1. Tahiliani M, et al. (2009) “Conversion of 5-methylcytosine to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine in mammalian DNA by MLL partner TET1.” Science 324(5929):930-5.

  2. Ito S, et al. (2011) “Tet proteins can convert 5-methylcytosine to 5-formylcytosine and 5-carboxylcytosine.” Science 333(6047):1300-3.

  3. He YF, et al. (2011) “Tet-mediated formation of 5-carboxylcytosine and its excision by TDG in mammalian DNA.” Science 333(6047):1303-7.

  4. Koh KP, et al. (2011) “Tet1 and Tet2 regulate 5-hydroxymethylcytosine production and cell lineage specification in mouse embryonic stem cells.” Cell Stem Cell 8(2):200-13.

  5. Dawlaty MM, et al. (2011) “Tet1 is dispensable for maintaining pluripotency and its loss is compatible with embryonic and postnatal development.” Cell Stem Cell 9(2):166-75.
entry.summary: A reflection on how the published TET literature changed the way I think about DNA methylation and gene regulation.

entry.title: Reading Glioblastoma ecDNA at Single-Cell Resolution

link.title: Reading Glioblastoma ecDNA at Single-Cell Resolution

entry.content:
Extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) consists of DNA circles separate from linear chromosomes. These circles can carry oncogenes and regulatory elements. Because ecDNA copy number can vary among tumor cells, it is one source of intratumoral heterogeneity. I wanted to understand how researchers can study that heterogeneity when the available data are single-cell chromatin accessibility profiles.

In a 2025 Cell Discovery paper, Jiang and colleagues introduce scCirclehunter, a computational framework that identifies candidate ecDNA regions from single-cell ATAC-seq data and assigns them to cell populations. The method uses a pseudo-bulk strategy and relies on assumptions about ecDNA copy number and chromatin accessibility. Its assignments are computational inferences from the sequencing data, not direct imaging of each circle in every cell.

What the study reports

The authors applied scCirclehunter to glioblastoma datasets and reported variation in ecDNA-bearing cell populations across patients. In a tumor with multiple ecDNAs, they used the framework to examine malignant-cell trajectories associated with different ecDNA species.

They also integrated single-cell RNA-seq data and focused on ecNR2E1. Their analyses linked ecNR2E1-bearing cells with broader transcriptional programs, and the authors interpret the results as evidence that ecDNA can contribute to tumor progression. They additionally report a potential association between ecDNA and increased mitochondrial transfer. The latter is presented as a possible link, not proof that ecDNA-bearing cells cause mitochondrial transfer.

What I took from it

The paper is a useful example of how an existing assay can support questions beyond its original readout. ATAC-seq measures accessible chromatin, but the authors use its signal patterns to infer candidate ecDNA and assign them to cell populations. That makes the method interesting for reanalysis of existing datasets, while also making validation and attention to its assumptions important.

I would be cautious about translating these results directly into clinical claims. The study offers a framework for investigating ecDNA-associated heterogeneity; it does not establish a biopsy strategy, a treatment, or a clinically validated way to select patients.

References

  1. Jiang R, et al. scCirclehunter delineates ecDNA-containing cells using single-cell ATAC-seq, with a focus on glioblastoma. Cell Discovery. 2025;11:98. doi:10.1038/s41421-025-00842-9
  2. Bailey C, Pich O, Thol K, et al. Origins and impact of extrachromosomal DNA. Nature. 2024;635:193-200.
entry.summary: What scCirclehunter can infer about ecDNA-bearing cell populations in glioblastoma from single-cell ATAC-seq data.

entry.title: Reading Epigenomic Changes Across Alzheimer’s Disease

link.title: Reading Epigenomic Changes Across Alzheimer’s Disease

entry.content:
Alzheimer’s disease is usually introduced through its defining pathology and its progressive cognitive effects. I have been interested in what epigenomic measurements can add to that picture: which regulatory features change across cell types and brain regions, and how those changes relate to disease progression.

A 2025 Cell study by Liu and colleagues addresses this question with single-nucleus epigenomic and transcriptomic data from six brain regions. The authors integrated ATAC-seq, RNA-seq and multiome datasets from aged control and Alzheimer’s disease donors. The scale is valuable, but the central contribution is the ability to compare regulatory patterns across regions and cell populations rather than treating the brain as a single sample.

What the study reports

The authors report widespread changes in large-scale chromatin compartmentalization and a reduction in what they define as single-cell epigenomic information. These are measurements of regulatory organization and cell-type-associated patterns; they should not be read as direct evidence that a cell has literally lost its identity.

The changes differed across brain regions and cell types. The study describes epigenomic information loss in several neuronal and glial populations, and reports that glial patterns vary with disease stage. I found this regional and cell-type specificity important: a bulk measurement could average together populations changing in different ways.

The paper also compares donors with different cognitive outcomes relative to their Alzheimer’s pathology. Higher epigenomic stability was associated with cognitive resilience in the analyzed data. That association is intriguing, but it does not establish that preserving epigenomic stability causes resilience or that a specific intervention can produce it.

What I took from it

The paper changed the question I ask of an epigenomic atlas. It is not only “which genes or regions change?” but also “which cell populations change, where, and in relation to what clinical or pathological measures?” The multiregion design makes those comparisons possible, while the observational nature of postmortem data sets limits on causal interpretation.

The authors discuss candidate regulatory mechanisms and future therapeutic directions. I read these as hypotheses for follow-up, not as evidence that Polycomb activity or another pathway is ready to be targeted to preserve cognition. The most useful contribution for now is the map of cell- and region-specific associations and the questions it makes possible.

Reference

  • Liu Z, et al. Single-cell multiregion epigenomic rewiring in Alzheimer’s disease progression and cognitive resilience. Cell. 2025;188(18):4980-5002.e29. doi:10.1016/j.cell.2025.06.031
entry.summary: What a multiregion single-cell study suggests about epigenomic changes, cell identity and cognitive resilience in Alzheimer's disease.
